A.claim: Any signed-in user can read any other user's allocation record and name by changing the user id in the /allocations/:userId path, because the handler uses the path id without comparing it to the session user and ids are sequential.
A non-admin signed-in user could reach the /benefits admin pages if the admin gate were missing; the gate is still wired.
A non-admin user denied access to an admin route receives a redirect instead of a 403 response.
Any signed-in user can read every memo posted by any user, because the memo listing returns all memos with no owner filter.
An unauthenticated visitor can reach the /tutorial pages because they have no login check.
A demoted admin could keep admin access if the admin middleware trusted a stale admin flag.
A new user could make themselves admin by sending an isAdmin field at signup (mass assignment).
A signed-in user could read or change another user's profile, contributions or dashboard data through these routes.
A caller of POST /benefits controls the target userId in the request body and can change any user's benefits record.
An admin can view any other user's allocations through /allocations/:userId; whether admins should keep this is undecided.
Memo content posted by one user may execute as script in other users' browsers (stored cross-site scripting).
Any caller can be sent to an attacker-chosen external URL through /learn (open redirect).
Any signed-in user can execute arbitrary server-side code because request-body fields are passed to eval.
A signed-in user can inject a NoSQL $where expression through the threshold parameter, which also bypasses the per-user filter.
An attacker can fix a victim's session id before login because the session is not regenerated at login.
Anyone who obtains the user store can read every password because passwords are stored in plaintext.
The session cookie can be read by scripts or sent over plain HTTP and does not expire, because it lacks httpOnly, secure and maxAge.
A cross-site page can make state-changing requests on behalf of a signed-in user because CSRF protection is disabled.

B.claim: Any signed-in user can read any other user's allocations and names by changing the user id in the /allocations/:userId path, because the handler uses the path id without comparing it to the session user and ids are sequential.
An attacker who plants a pre-login session cookie in a victim's browser gains the victim's (including an admin's) authenticated session, because login does not regenerate the session id.
The admin middleware ignores a database error when loading the user, which could affect the admin access decision.
A non-admin signed-in user could bypass the /benefits admin gate and read or change benefits data.
A non-admin user denied access to an admin route receives a redirect instead of a 403 response.
A new user could make themselves admin through signup by supplying an admin flag.
A signed-in user could make themselves admin through a profile update by supplying an admin field.
Any signed-in user can read every memo because memos are returned to all users with no owner.
An unauthenticated visitor can reach / because the route has no middleware.
An unauthenticated visitor can reach the /tutorial pages because they have no login check.
Any signed-in user can execute arbitrary server-side code because contribution fields are passed to eval.
A signed-in user can inject into a $where expression via threshold and widen the allocations query beyond one user.
A signed-in user can make the server send requests to arbitrary destinations via the url and symbol parameters (SSRF).
Any caller can be sent to an attacker-chosen external URL through /learn (open redirect).
Anyone who obtains the user store can read every password because passwords are stored and compared in plaintext.
A cross-site page can make state-changing requests on behalf of a signed-in user because the CSRF middleware is commented out.
An unauthenticated caller can learn which usernames exist because login returns distinct error messages.

A signed-in user can make the server send requests to a user-supplied URL (SSRF).

Memo content posted by one user can execute as script in other users' browsers because template autoescaping is off when memos render (stored XSS).

An attacker can fix a victim's session id before login because the session is not regenerated at login.
The session cookie can be read by scripts or sent insecurely because it is set without security flags.
